text:
## Abstract  
Staphylococcus aureus is one of the most intensively studied bacterial pathogens, yet large-scale data resources differ in both the amount and the kind of information they archive. We quantified and contrasted all S. aureus records in two major public repositories: NCBI’s Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), which stores processed functional‐genomics datasets, and the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA), which hosts raw sequencing runs. Taxonomy ID 1280 (Staphylococcus aureus) was first resolved with NCBI Taxonomy. GEO was queried four times—once for each record class—returning 500 Series (GSE), 5 464 Samples (GSM), 176 Platforms (GPL), and 12 curated DataSets (GDS). ENA was accessed through the BRC Analytics proxy; the call reported 181 408 sequencing runs for the same taxon. These numbers show that ENA’s raw read archive for S. aureus is two orders of magnitude larger than GEO’s processed expression holdings. The result highlights how raw data generation has outpaced downstream processing and curation for this species, informing researchers where to look first depending on whether they need expression matrices or primary reads.

## I. Introduction  
Background. Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive opportunistic pathogen responsible for a wide spectrum of human infections and renowned for its antibiotic resistance. Functional-genomics studies (GEO) and raw read archives (ENA) are complementary resources for investigating its biology.  
Literature Review. No literature was retrieved for this query.  
Knowledge Gap. The relative scale of S. aureus coverage in GEO versus ENA had not been quantified side-by-side.  
Objective & Hypothesis. We aimed to enumerate S. aureus-specific records in GEO and ENA. We expected ENA, as a raw-read repository, to contain substantially more records than GEO.

## II. Materials and Methods  
Study Design. Counts were obtained independently from GEO (processed-data repository) and ENA (raw-data repository) using repository-specific APIs.  
Materials.  
• NCBI Taxonomy via ncbi_taxonomy_lookup  
• GEO via geo_search  
• ENA via brc_ena_runs  
Procedures.  
1. ncbi_taxonomy_lookup (query="Staphylococcus aureus") → taxid 1280.  
2. geo_search (organism="Staphylococcus aureus", entry_type="gse", max_results=0) → total_count.  
3. geo_search (organism="Staphylococcus aureus", entry_type="gsm", max_results=0) → total_count.  
4. geo_search (organism="Staphylococcus aureus", entry_type="gpl", max_results=0) → total_count.  
5. geo_search (organism="Staphylococcus aureus", entry_type="gds", max_results=0) → total_count.  
6. brc_ena_runs (taxonomy_id="1280", limit=1) → total_in_ena.  
Statistical Analysis. Each GEO call returns `total_count`; no deduplication is required because record classes are mutually exclusive. The ENA call reports `total_in_ena`, representing unique run accessions. Percentages were calculated with the denominator set to ENA run count when comparing relative scale.

## III. Results  
Data Presentation.  
Table 1. Repository coverage for Staphylococcus aureus (taxid 1280)

| Repository | Record class (API field) | Count |
|------------|--------------------------|-------|
| GEO        | Series (GSE)             | 500   |
| GEO        | Samples (GSM)            | 5 464 |
| GEO        | Platforms (GPL)          | 176   |
| GEO        | Curated DataSets (GDS)   | 12    |
| ENA        | Sequencing runs          | 181 408 |

Findings. GEO contains 500 Series encompassing 5 464 individual samples and 176 distinct microarray or sequencing platforms, plus 12 legacy curated DataSets. ENA archives 181 408 raw sequencing runs for S. aureus. Thus, raw runs outnumber GEO Series by ~360-fold and GEO Samples by ~33-fold.

## IV. Discussion  
Interpretation. ENA’s S. aureus collection vastly exceeds GEO’s in record count, reflecting heavy deposition of primary reads relative to processed expression data. GEO’s 500 Series—while valuable for hypothesis testing—represent a small subset of available experiments.  
Context. The disparity aligns with trends where raw read submission is mandatory for publication, whereas processed transcriptomic datasets require additional curation and remain optional.  
Limitations. GEO counts do not equate to unique studies because one study may split across multiple Series; ENA counts individual runs, not studies. No quality metrics were assessed.  
Conclusion & Future Directions. Researchers needing omics data on S. aureus should begin with ENA for raw reads and with GEO for curated expression matrices. Future work could enumerate distinct ENA BioProjects to refine study-level comparisons and assess overlap between repositories.

## References  
[1] NCBI Taxonomy. https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?term=Staphylococcus+aureus&retmax=50&retstart=0&sort=relevance&retmode=json&db=taxonomy&tool=fdea-ncbi-mcp&email=jonathangunti%40gmail.com  
[2] GEO GSE count. https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=%22Staphylococcus%20aureus%22%5BOrganism%5D%20AND%20%22gse%22%5BFilter%5D&retmax=1  
[3] GEO GSM count. https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=%22Staphylococcus%20aureus%22%5BOrganism%5D%20AND%20%22gsm%22%5BFilter%5D&retmax=1  
[4] GEO GPL count. https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=%22Staphylococcus%20aureus%22%5BOrganism%5D%20AND%20%22gpl%22%5BFilter%5D&retmax=1  
[5] GEO GDS count. https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=%22Staphylococcus%20aureus%22%5BOrganism%5D%20AND%20%22gds%22%5BFilter%5D&retmax=1  
[6] ENA run count (via BRC Analytics). https://brc-analytics.org/api/v1/ena/taxonomy/1280?limit=1  

## Acknowledgments  
Data were retrieved from NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), NCBI Taxonomy, and the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) via BRC Analytics.
